title: Combination
body:
A **combination** is a selection where **order does not matter**. Choosing $r$ items from
$n$ distinct items, caring only which ones you got:

$$C(n, r) = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$$

Read $\binom{n}{r}$ as "$n$ choose $r$". A combination is a subset, so this is counting
subsets of a given size, which ties it straight back to [[Sets]].

The formula is derived, not invented. Count the ordered version first, then remove the
ordering you did not want:

$$C(n, r) = \frac{P(n, r)}{r!}$$

Every unordered selection of $r$ items was counted $r!$ times by [[Permutation]], once per
arrangement, so divide it out.

```
5 people, how many ways to pick a 3-person committee?
    order does not matter (a committee is a set)
    C(5, 3) = 5!/(3! · 2!) = 10

Compare P(5, 3) = 60.  Same selections, 3! = 6 orderings each.
```

## Identities worth knowing

- $C(n, r) = C(n, n-r)$. Choosing which 3 of 5 to take is the same act as choosing which 2
  to leave behind, so the counts are equal. Use it to make the arithmetic smaller:
  $C(20, 18)$ is $C(20, 2) = 190$.
- $C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1$. There is one way to take nothing and one way to take everything.
- $\sum_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) = 2^n$. Summing subsets of every size gives all subsets, which is
  the power-set count from [[Sets]].
- Pascal's rule: $C(n, r) = C(n-1, r-1) + C(n-1, r)$. Either the first item is in your
  selection or it is not. This is a recurrence, and it is the standard first exercise in
  proving something by [[Proof By Induction]].

## Why it matters for CS

Counting is how you size a problem before you try to solve it. "How many subsets does this
algorithm have to consider" is a combination question, and $2^n$ subsets is the reason
subset-style problems land in [[NP-Complete]] and why brute force stops being an option
around $n = 30$. On the other side, the $\log n$ in [[Time Complexity]] bounds is always
the same fact read backwards: halving the search space $\log n$ times exhausts it, which is
why [[Binary Search Tree]] lookup is cheap.

$\binom{n}{k}$ also turns up as a coefficient rather than a count. The binomial distribution's
$P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ in [[Probability Distribution]] uses it to count how many
sequences of $n$ trials contain $k$ successes, which is this note doing its ordinary job inside a
[[STATISTICS]] formula.
